passage:
Dear Ritu,
Thanks for asking how I finished the sociology paper without my usual meltdown. Here is the boring truth. On Monday I wrote a terrible draft in about ninety minutes, no deleting, bad sentences and all, with "[find number]" in brackets wherever I was unsure. Then I closed the file and went out. I did not look at it on Tuesday or Wednesday. On Thursday I printed it and read it slowly, marking three things: my main point, what was missing, what could go. A whole page went. Only after that did I fix sentences. On Friday I submitted with time to spare. Before, I would rewrite my first paragraph eleven times. Try it on your report.
Zainab

qa.q: How long did Zainab take to write the first draft on Monday?
What was Zainab probably feeling in earlier essays when rewriting the first paragraph eleven times?
qa.a: Anxious and stuck, wanting every sentence to be perfect before moving on.

qa.q: Why was leaving the file alone on Tuesday and Wednesday a smart step?
qa.a: It let Zainab return on Thursday with fresh eyes and edit clearly, instead of polishing while still creating.

qa.q: What might Ritu be facing that made Zainab share this method?
qa.a: Ritu is probably working on a report and is stuck as Zainab used to be, since Zainab ends with "Try it on your report."

grounding: Shows a writer who drafts roughly without judging, rests, then edits with fresh eyes.

passage: Right, Chaitanya, the honest version. I'm Seema, and for my final-year project report I used to open the file and fix the first line for two hours. So this time I split the job. Mornings were for creating only. I set a timer for forty minutes, typed badly, left gaps like "add example here", and did not even fix spelling. I did that for five days. Then I went home for the weekend, played cricket with my cousins and did not open the file once. On Sunday night I read it on my phone like a stranger would. Whole paragraphs repeated, and one page did not belong. Monday was editing with a red pen. I finished two days early, and I actually liked reading it.

qa.q: How long was Seema's timer set for each morning?
qa.a: Seema set the timer for forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Seema leave gaps like "add example here" instead of fixing them?
qa.a: Seema wanted to keep creating without judging, worried that stopping to polish would stall the draft.

qa.q: What did Seema do on Sunday night that made the edit work?
qa.a: Seema read the draft on a phone like a stranger would, and spotted repeated paragraphs and a page that did not belong.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya find surprising about Seema's method?
qa.a: Chaitanya might be surprised that Seema stopped editing while writing and rested for a weekend, the opposite of endless polishing. 🙂

grounding: Shows a writer who separates rough drafting from editing and rests between them.
